title: Clustered Randomized Smoothing for Stochastic Prediction Functions
claim: Standard smoothing averages multi-modal predictions into one region that misses every mode; smoothing each mode separately and mixing preserves them.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, same road scene with contour ellipses and labeled regions
description: Three side-by-side panels show the same top-down cross-junction scene. A red ego vehicle sits on the left, and a green vehicle sits at the upper right. Panel (a), 'base predictor', shows green contour ellipses at two places: the vehicle's current position, and the road below the junction after a curved arrow turns left. These are the two modes. Panel (b), 'randomized smoothing', shows one blue rotated box labeled R in the middle of the intersection. It holds a single averaged ellipse and covers neither mode. Panel (c), 'our approach', shows two small blue boxes, R1 at the vehicle's position and R2 on the lower road. They are labeled R = R1 ∪ R2, so each mode is kept. Dark blue math labels and green contours stand out against the black road lines and the red and green cars.
caption: Conceptual illustration of mode collapse in randomized smoothing. In (a), an ego vehicle (red) is predicting the trajectory of another vehicle (green) at a cross junction. The stochastic predictor outputs a distribution with two modes: turning left before the ego vehicle passes the intersection, or waiting for it to pass before initiating the turn. In (b), current randomized smoothing methods (e.g., [30]) would produce an averaged prediction, failing to capture any of the two modes. Instead, in (c), our approach is to smooth each mode individually and combine as a mixture model, which preserves the modes corresponding to the two tactical behaviors. Sets R represent the sets that can be certified with each method.
abstract: Modern stochastic predictors can model rich, multi-modal outcome distributions. However, this expressive power comes with challenges in ensuring robust predictions $-$ a critical requirement in safety-critical domains. Randomized smoothing is a leading technique for improving robustness, particularly against adversarial perturbations. Yet, in stochastic multi-modal regression settings, randomized smoothing often fails due to mode collapse, yielding averaged predictions that do not reflect the underlying distribution. To address this limitation, we propose clustered $Î±$-smoothing, a framework that (1) partitions noisy samples using an arbitrary clustering algorithm, (2) applies $Î±$-smoothing locally within each cluster, and (3) combines the resulting predictions into a mixture distribution. By interpreting the smoothing distribution as a mixture of $Î±$-smoothers, we derive a lower bound on the probability that the smoothed prediction lies within a union of compact regions corresponding to distinct modes. We empirically evaluate our framework on two benchmarks, demonstrating substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods. In stochastic trajectory prediction on a driving simulator dataset, our approach achieves, on average, a $27\%$ lower Wasserstein distance to the ground-truth distribution compared to $Î±$-smoothing. In quadrotor control, where modes correspond to distinct feasible paths to a target, our method reduces the collision rate by $90\%$ relative to the state-of-the-art randomized smoothing.
